description: We are a team of college students interested in creating space based projects which make an impact.
summary:
Astro Health was created by Team Callsign: ORBIT for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026.
Astro Health is an offline‑first diagnostic engine for astronaut health built for deep space missions. We built a Progressive Web App that uses React, TypeScript and Python machine learning. This app has a SVG body map and a two‑minute daily check‑in.
Astro Health solves the mission challenge by taking data from many sensors and running it through automatic quality checks for range and noise. Astro Health compares the data to a fourteen‑day baseline using z‑scores and tracks persistence. Astro Health then puts each astronaut in one of three categories: Normal, Watch or Act. Astro Health gives plain‑language reasons for each category. Suggests preventive actions.
This is very important because deep space missions have communication delays of three to twenty‑two minutes and no quick evacuation option. Astronauts must manage their health. Astro Health supplies full on‑device autonomy working locally after the install. Astro Health also flags changes in health two days before traditional alerts. Astro Health creates automated summary reports, for ground flight surgeons using a transparent deterministic rules engine instead of unverified artificial intelligence language models.
details:
Astro Health (developed by Team Callsign: ORBIT for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026) is a first sensor-agnostic astronaut health diagnostic engine. Built as a Progressive Web App (PWA) it enables non-physician crew members on deep-space missions to monitor their own health and receive actionable preventive guidance without needing an active network connection.

What It Does and How It Works

Astro Health operates through a five-stage on-device pipeline:

Sense: Ingests telemetry from Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) and USB devices alongside manual inputs from a 2-minute daily check-in tracking vitals such as heart rate, blood pressure, SpO2, temperature, cabin CO2, sleep duration and mood.

Quality Gate: Filters readings for range violations signal noise and timestamp consistency to prevent false alarms.

Store: Saves time-stamped metrics locally on the device.

Decide: Evaluates readings using a rules-first engine that combines absolute safety thresholds 14-day personal baseline z-scores, persistence checks (3+ days outside normal) and multi-symptom pattern rules (such as combined shifts in heart rate, sleep and mood).

Present: Translates results into a clickable SVG human body map categorized into three clear tiers—Normal (continue routine) Watch (take preventive action) and Act (contact flight surgeon)—complete with plain-language explanations and an auto-generated summary report for flight surgeons.

Intended Impact

Complete Deep-Space Autonomy: Because assistance on Moon and Mars missions is 3 to 22 minutes away with no immediate evacuation options running 100% locally after installation allows astronauts to serve immediately as their own first line of medical care.

Earlier Anomaly Detection: By tracking baseline drift and multi-day persistence rather than waiting for extreme threshold breaches the system flags physiological drift approximately 2 days earlier.

Reduced Crew Cognitive Load: Non-physician crew members spend 2 minutes a day on check-ins and receive clear plain-language preventive guidance, such as breathing exercises or scheduling a family call.

Streamlined Ground Support: Flight surgeons receive structured -analyzed summary reports whenever communication links sync enabling faster response times reduced risk and stronger crew resilience.

Tools, Languages, Hardware and Software Used

Frontend and App Framework: React, TypeScript, Vite PWA, Zustand and a custom interactive SVG body map.

Backend, Analytics and Storage: Python scikit-learn, statsmodels, FastAPI and local SQLite storage.

Protocols: Designed to interface with BLE and USB sensors using standard protocols such as the Bluetooth Heart Rate Profile.

NASA. Standards: Built upon the NASA Human Research Programs 5 Hazards Roadmap, Spaceflight Standard Measures, Artemis II Standard Measures, the NASA Twins Study and NASA-STD-3001 crew health standards.

Creativity and Key Design Factors Considered

AI Safety and Explainability: than allowing black-box Large Language Models (LLMs) to make high-risk medical calls the team engineered a transparent deterministic rules-first engine backed by statistical baseline modeling so every alert is auditable and reliable.

Hazard-to-Indicator Mapping: The team mapped NASAs five hazards (radiation, isolation, distance, gravity and hostile closed habitats) directly to measurable physiological and behavioral indicators.

Small-Sample Validation and Hardware Agnosticism: Recognizing that spaceflight datasets are hardware evolves, across missions the team validated its baseline methods using Leave-One-Astronaut-Out (LOAO) cross-validation on synthetic crew data and built sensor-agnostic adapters that run in any modern browser.
